## S1. Search strategy

| Field | Content |
|:---|:---|
| Databases searched | PubMed/MEDLINE, EMBASE (Elsevier), SCOPUS |
| Search dates | Database inception to January 1999-April 2026 |
| Records retrieved | PubMed 1061; EMBASE 2603; SCOPUS 481 (total 4145) |
| Date limits applied | January 1999-April 2026 |
| Language limit | English |
| Publication types excluded via filter | None. Conference abstracts, editorials, letters, and case reports were excluded at screening rather than by search filter, to minimise inappropriate exclusion |
| Other sources searched | Reference list screening of included studies and prior systematic reviews; forward citation tracking (Web of Science) for key index publications; PROSPERO search for related and ongoing reviews |
| Deduplication and management | RIS export from each database, imported into Covidence for deduplication and screening |
| Search piloted against | Eight known included publications (Holtan 2022, Moiseev 2016, Tang 2023, Papanicolaou 2023, Salas 2023, Massoud 2021, Meyer 2024, Shaffer 2024) to verify recall |

: Search parameters.

The protocol specifies three concept blocks combined with AND, each block an OR of controlled vocabulary terms and free-text synonyms.

### PubMed/MEDLINE

```         
#1  Allogeneic HCT population
    ("Hematopoietic Stem Cell Transplantation"[Mesh] OR "Bone Marrow Transplantation"[Mesh]
     OR "allogeneic stem cell transplant*"[tiab] OR "allo-HCT"[tiab] OR "allo-HSCT"[tiab]
     OR "haploidentical"[tiab] OR "HLA-matched"[tiab] OR "matched unrelated donor"[tiab]
     OR "mismatched unrelated donor"[tiab])

#2  PTCy intervention
    ("post-transplant cyclophosphamide"[tiab] OR "post-transplantation cyclophosphamide"[tiab]
     OR "posttransplant cyclophosphamide"[tiab] OR "posttransplantation cyclophosphamide"[tiab]
     OR "PTCy"[tiab] OR "PT-Cy"[tiab] OR "PTCY"[tiab]
     OR ("Cyclophosphamide"[Mesh] AND "Graft vs Host Disease"[Mesh]))

#3  Infection outcomes
    ("Infections"[Mesh] OR "Bacterial Infections"[Mesh] OR "Virus Diseases"[Mesh]
     OR "Mycoses"[Mesh] OR "Bacteremia"[Mesh] OR "Sepsis"[Mesh]
     OR "Cytomegalovirus Infections"[Mesh] OR "Invasive Fungal Infections"[Mesh]
     OR "bacterial infection*"[tiab] OR "viral infection*"[tiab] OR "fungal infection*"[tiab]
     OR "BSI"[tiab] OR "sepsis"[tiab] OR "CMV"[tiab] OR "EBV"[tiab] OR "HHV-6"[tiab]
     OR "BK virus"[tiab] OR "aspergillosis"[tiab] OR "candida"[tiab] OR "mucormycosis"[tiab]
     OR "mold"[tiab] OR "yeast"[tiab] OR "mortality"[tiab])

#4  #1 AND #2 AND #3
    Filters: Humans; English
```

### EMBASE (Emtree)

```         
#1  Allogeneic HCT population
    ('bone marrow transplantation'/exp OR 'stem cell transplantation'/exp
     OR 'allogeneic stem cell transplant*':ti,ab OR 'allo-hct':ti,ab OR 'allo-hsct':ti,ab
     OR haploidentical:ti,ab OR 'hla-matched':ti,ab OR 'matched unrelated donor':ti,ab
     OR 'mismatched unrelated donor':ti,ab)

#2  PTCy intervention
    ('post-transplant cyclophosphamide':ti,ab OR 'post-transplantation cyclophosphamide':ti,ab
     OR 'posttransplant cyclophosphamide':ti,ab OR 'posttransplantation cyclophosphamide':ti,ab
     OR ptcy:ti,ab OR 'pt-cy':ti,ab
     OR ('cyclophosphamide'/exp AND 'graft versus host reaction'/exp))

#3  Infection outcomes
    ('infection'/exp OR 'bacterial infection'/exp OR 'virus infection'/exp OR 'mycosis'/exp
     OR 'bacteremia'/exp OR 'sepsis'/exp OR 'cytomegalovirus infection'/exp
     OR 'invasive fungal infection'/exp
     OR 'bacterial infection*':ti,ab OR 'viral infection*':ti,ab OR 'fungal infection*':ti,ab
     OR bsi:ti,ab OR sepsis:ti,ab OR cmv:ti,ab OR ebv:ti,ab OR 'hhv-6':ti,ab
     OR 'bk virus':ti,ab OR aspergillosis:ti,ab OR candida:ti,ab OR mucormycosis:ti,ab
     OR mold:ti,ab OR yeast:ti,ab OR mortality:ti,ab)

#4  #1 AND #2 AND #3 AND [humans]/lim AND [english]/lim
```

### SCOPUS

```         
TITLE-ABS-KEY(
  ("allogeneic stem cell transplant*" OR "allo-HCT" OR "allo-HSCT"
   OR "hematopoietic stem cell transplantation" OR "bone marrow transplantation"
   OR haploidentical OR "HLA-matched" OR "matched unrelated donor"
   OR "mismatched unrelated donor")
  AND
  ("post-transplant cyclophosphamide" OR "post-transplantation cyclophosphamide"
   OR "posttransplant cyclophosphamide" OR "posttransplantation cyclophosphamide"
   OR PTCy OR "PT-Cy" OR (cyclophosphamide AND "graft versus host disease"))
  AND
  (infection* OR "bacterial infection*" OR "viral infection*" OR "fungal infection*"
   OR BSI OR sepsis OR bacteremia OR CMV OR "cytomegalovirus infection*" OR EBV
   OR "HHV-6" OR "BK virus" OR aspergillosis OR candida OR mucormycosis OR mold
   OR yeast OR "invasive fungal infection*" OR mortality)
) AND LANGUAGE(english)
```

| Domain                                    | Low | Moderate | Serious |
|:------------------------------------------|----:|---------:|--------:|
| D1 Confounding                            |   0 |       86 |     134 |
| D2 Selection of participants              |  30 |      142 |      46 |
| D3 Classification of interventions        |  53 |      162 |       5 |
| D4 Deviations from intended interventions | 199 |       20 |       0 |
| D5 Missing data                           |  72 |      147 |       1 |
| D6 Measurement of outcomes                | 104 |      105 |       4 |
| D7 Selection of the reported result       | 166 |       46 |       1 |

: ROBINS-I domain-level risk of bias, counts by judgement (n = 220 comparative observational studies; single-arm descriptive studies protocol-excluded without judgement). D6 and D7 were not recorded for the same 7 studies, so those rows sum to 213; the overall judgements (serious 149, moderate 71) are recorded for all 220 studies.

![ROBINS-I traffic-light plot for all comparative observational studies.](figures/FigureS5a_ROBINS_traffic_light){#fig-s5a}

![ROBINS-I domain-level summary.](figures/FigureS5b_ROBINS_domain_summary){#fig-s5b}

![RoB 2 summary for the 14 randomised controlled trials.](figures/FigureS5c_RoB2_summary){#fig-s5c}

Because the RoB 2 measurement-of-outcome domain (D4) is most consequential for subjective endpoints, the 14 trial assessments were reviewed by outcome objectivity. For objective outcomes — overall survival, non-relapse and relapse-related mortality, and laboratory-confirmed bloodstream infection — measurement-domain risk was low in all 14 trials. For subjective, clinician-assessed outcomes — acute and chronic GVHD grading and adjudication of infection episodes — 3 of 14 trials had some concerns in the measurement domain because outcome assessors were unblinded to allocation (studies 2, 105 and 465). Two trials were at high overall risk: one for deviations from the assigned randomised regimen (study 432, D2) and one for baseline imbalances suggestive of randomisation problems (study 72, D1). These judgements support treating the trials' mortality and virological endpoints as more dependable than their GVHD endpoints.

Full justification narratives are available in `rob.csv`, submitted as a supplementary data file.

## S6. Model specification and priors

Primary model (M1), for study $s$, arm $i$:

$$\text{events}_i \mid n_i \sim \text{Binomial}\!\left(n_i,\ \text{logit}^{-1}\!\left(\alpha + \big(\beta_{\text{PTCy}} + v_{s[i]}\big)\, x_i + \beta_{\text{tp}}\, t_i + u_{s[i]}\right)\right),
\qquad (u_s, v_s) \sim \mathcal{N}_2(\mathbf{0}, \boldsymbol{\Sigma})$$

where $x_i$ indicates a PTCy arm and $t_i$ indicates that the study contributed a fallback timepoint rather than the outcome's preferred timepoint (day +100 or +180 for early outcomes, one year for late outcomes). Each study contributes exactly one row per outcome — the preferred timepoint when reported, otherwise the nearest reported timepoint — so no within-study correlation across timepoints arises. Each study contributes a random intercept $u_s$ (baseline-risk variation) and a random PTCy-effect slope $v_s$, so the pooled coefficient $\beta_{\text{PTCy}}$ estimates the average study-level treatment effect and the between-study SD of $v_s$ (reported as τ) quantifies heterogeneity in the PTCy effect. With two arms per study the model is just-identified at study level, so for sparse outcomes (k ≤ 6) the prior on the SD parameters is correspondingly influential.

| Parameter                   | Prior                    |
|:----------------------------|:-------------------------|
| Fixed effects (β)           | N(0, 2·5)                |
| Intercept (α)               | N(0, 1·5)                |
| Between-study SDs (τ)       | Student t(3, 0, 1), half |
| Intercept–slope correlation | LKJ(1)                   |

: Prior specification for the primary model.

The exploratory steroid-adjustment model (M2; a post-hoc protocol amendment, S13) adds arm-level systemic corticosteroid exposure, mean-centred, as an additional fixed effect, and is fitted on the complete-case subset of studies with exposure data (C1 OS 27/34, C1 RRM 27/34, C1 NRM 9/12, C1 CMV 18/22, C2 OS 8/9, C2 CMV 12/12). M2 is reported only in this supplement: its definition, provenance, results, and limitations are given in S9.

MCMC: four chains × 4000 iterations (1000 warmup), `adapt_delta` = 0·95 (increased to 0·99 where divergent transitions occurred), giving 12 000 post-warmup draws per model.

## S9. Sensitivity analyses

![CMV sensitivity models, comparison 1: primary model, post-2020 restriction, and haploidentical-dominant restriction.](figures/FigureS9a_CMV_sensitivity){#fig-s9a}

![IFI leave-one-out analysis, comparison 1 (frequentist REML).](figures/FigureS9b_IFI_leave_one_out){#fig-s9b}

In the originally submitted analysis the largest Bayesian–frequentist discrepancies were for C1 bloodstream infection (Bayesian odds ratio 1·87 \[1·33–2·62\] versus REML 1·29 \[0·61–2·73\]) and C1 invasive fungal infection (0·43 \[0·29–0·63\] versus 0·60 \[0·21–1·74\]). These gaps were not caused by the N(0, 2·5) priors on the regression coefficients, which are weak relative to the binomial likelihood even at k = 6. They arose because the submitted models fixed the treatment effect across studies (a common-effect specification) while the REML concordance models estimate a between-study variance, and heterogeneity is substantial for both outcomes (I² = 71% and 80%). A common-effect and a random-effects model answer different questions when heterogeneity is present, and at k = 6 the discrepancy is stark. Under the adopted random-slope specification, which — like REML — allows the treatment effect to vary across studies, the two approaches agree closely (BSI: Bayesian 1·42 \[0·57–2·98\] versus REML 1·29 \[0·61–2·73\]; IFI: 0·63 \[0·19–2·62\] versus 0·60 \[0·21–1·74\]). Residual differences across outcomes reflect the different likelihoods (arm-level binomial versus two-stage normal approximation with a 0·5 continuity correction) and the Bayesian propagation of τ uncertainty into wider intervals, not the coefficient priors; the τ-prior sensitivity analysis below confirms that the prior on the between-study SD has little influence even at k = 6.

### τ-prior sensitivity for the k = 6 outcomes

For C1 BSI and C1 IFI (k = 6), where the Student t(3, 0, 1) prior on the between-study SDs is most influential, the random-slope M1 models were refitted with a narrower (t(3, 0, 0·5)) and a wider (t(3, 0, 2)) SD prior, all other settings unchanged. The pooled odds ratios and their intervals shift little across a fourfold change in prior scale, and no conclusion changes, so these estimates are driven by the likelihood rather than the τ prior.

| Outcome | SD prior          | OR (95% CrI)     | τ (slope SD, posterior median) |
|:--------|:------------------|:-----------------|-------------------------------:|
| C1 BSI  | t(3, 0, 0·5)      | 1·49 (0·68–2·72) |                           0·56 |
| C1 BSI  | t(3, 0, 1) — base | 1·42 (0·57–2·98) |                           0·72 |
| C1 BSI  | t(3, 0, 2)        | 1·37 (0·48–3·22) |                           0·85 |
| C1 IFI  | t(3, 0, 0·5)      | 0·59 (0·23–1·95) |                           1·03 |
| C1 IFI  | t(3, 0, 1) — base | 0·63 (0·19–2·62) |                           1·28 |
| C1 IFI  | t(3, 0, 2)        | 0·65 (0·17–3·53) |                           1·57 |

: τ-prior sensitivity for the two outcomes with k = 6. Fits and full posterior summaries are exported in `prior_sensitivity_tau.csv`, a supplementary data file.

### Fixed (stratified) study intercepts

The primary models use a random study intercept, under which the pooled treatment effect is estimated partly from between-study contrasts and within-study randomisation is not preserved [@senn2010]. As a sensitivity analysis, every model in Table 2 was refitted with fixed (stratified) study-specific intercepts and a random PTCy-effect slope, so that the treatment effect is identified solely from within-study contrasts, as in two-stage meta-analysis of odds ratios; priors and sampler settings were otherwise unchanged. Posterior median odds ratios were concordant: the median absolute shift on the log-odds-ratio scale across the 29 models was 0·03, no estimate changed direction, and 25 of 29 shifts were below 0·1. The largest shifts occurred in sparse or steroid-adjusted models — C1 NRM (M2): 0·81 \[0·27–1·57\] to 0·61 \[0·14–1·41\]; C1 IFI: 0·63 \[0·19–2·62\] to 0·54 \[0·16–1·85\]; C3 RRM: 0·78 \[0·35–1·73\] to 0·68 \[0·29–1·39\]; C1 OS (M2): 0·95 \[0·70–1·27\] to 0·86 \[0·60–1·19\]. Only one interval conclusion changed: C2 BK virus reactivation (k = 3), whose lower credible bound moved from 1·09 to 0·97 and so no longer excludes 1, an outcome already rated low certainty. Full per-model results are provided in `fe_sensitivity_setB.csv`, a supplementary data file.

Restricting the primary outcome to randomised trials is only weakly informative after cohort deduplication, which leaves two trials (odds ratio 0·73 \[0·17–3·42\]). An earlier estimate across seven randomised trials in the pre-deduplication C1 overall-survival dataset (0·79 \[0·59–1·08\]) was computed before cumulative-incidence-derived event counts were removed from pooling (2026-10-02; see the randomised-trials-only section below) and is superseded: with observed event counts only, at most two trials remain per outcome, so trial-only analyses are no longer estimable.

### Hazard-ratio sensitivity for overall survival

Overall survival was analysed as the odds ratio of death at fixed timepoints because most studies reported only event counts or Kaplan–Meier estimates at those timepoints; hazard ratios were available for a minority of studies, with heterogeneous covariate adjustment. In a post-hoc sensitivity analysis, one overall-survival hazard ratio per study was taken from the extraction database (multivariable-adjusted estimates preferred; the timepoint matching the analytic dataset preferred; direction harmonised to PTCy versus comparator with death as the event, inverting comparator-first estimates) and pooled two-stage in a Bayesian normal-normal random-effects model on log hazard ratios with known standard errors (same weakly-informative prior family as the primary models), with a frequentist REML concordance check.

For C1 (k = 14 of 34 studies, 13 adjusted) the pooled hazard ratio was 0·88 \[0·66–1·14\] (REML 0·88 \[0·69–1·12\]), versus the primary odds ratio of 0·76 \[0·61–0·93\]. For C2 (k = 4 of 9 studies, all adjusted) it was 0·60 \[0·26–1·08\] (REML 0·59 \[0·40–0·89\]), versus 0·75 \[0·42–1·31\]. The direction of effect is consistent across estimands, but the C1 hazard-ratio estimate is attenuated towards 1 relative to the odds ratio. Plausible contributors are the multivariable adjustment carried by nearly all hazard-ratio-reporting studies — which removes confounding that the raw-count odds ratio absorbs — the smaller, self-selected subset of studies reporting hazard ratios, and the different estimand (a whole-follow-up hazard ratio versus fixed-timepoint mortality odds). The C2 estimate is imprecise at k = 4, and its REML interval, which excludes 1, is optimistic relative to the Bayesian interval with so few studies. The per-study hazard ratios used are provided in `hr_sensitivity_os.csv`, a supplementary data file.

### Exploratory steroid-adjustment analysis (M2)

M2 was a post-hoc amendment to the registered protocol (S13) and is exploratory; it is reported only in this appendix. It adds arm-level systemic corticosteroid exposure, mean-centred, to the M1 specification. Steroid exposure was defined as the percentage of patients in each arm receiving systemic corticosteroids for graft-versus-host disease, as reported by the study at the study's own timepoint; where a study did not report exposure directly it was approximated from the arm's acute GVHD grade II–IV cumulative incidence under a pre-specified extraction rule. The database does not distinguish the two sources, but comparing exposure values against arm-level acute GVHD grade II–IV incidences shows that 175 of the 202 steroid-complete M2 arms (87%) carry values numerically identical to the arm's GVHD incidence (≤0·5 percentage points), so most M2 covariate values are the approximation rather than a direct report. Exposure could not be obtained for 127 of 523 arms (24%), so M2 is fitted on a complete-case subset for each outcome (studies with exposure data / all studies: C1 OS 27/34, C1 RRM 27/34, C1 NRM 9/12, C1 CMV 18/22, C2 OS 8/9, C2 CMV 12/12); no values were imputed by the model.

M2 is not a mediation analysis: it estimates no indirect effect, and because it adjusts for a post-treatment variable measured at arm level it is open to ecological bias and to collider bias — steroid use follows GVHD, which PTCy itself prevents, and may also mark other causes of death. Attenuation from M1 to M2 is therefore hypothesis-generating rather than evidence of mediation or confounding.

The reported M1 uses all studies with outcome data, whereas M2 drops studies without exposure data, so an M1–M2 contrast mixes covariate adjustment with a changed study set. M1 was therefore refitted — specification and priors unchanged — on each outcome's M2 complete-case subset. For C1 overall survival the attenuation is attributable to the covariate rather than the subset: on the same 27 studies M1 gives 0·77 (0·59–0·97) and M2 gives 0·95 (0·70–1·27), against a full-set M1 of 0·76 (0·61–0·93). The same pattern holds for C2 overall survival (matched-set M1 0·69 \[0·36–1·30\] versus M2 0·90 \[0·45–1·74\]). Conversely, the C1 relapse-related-mortality interval crossing the null after steroid adjustment is attributable to the subset rather than the covariate (matched-set M1 0·87 \[0·73–1·02\]; M2 0·85 \[0·71–1·02\]). Fits and per-model summaries are exported in `m1_m2_matched.csv`, a supplementary data file.

### Donor-type confounding

PTCy arms are enriched for haploidentical recipients (47% versus 15% of comparator arms overall). Two analyses address the resulting confounding concern for the five main C1 outcomes, refitted 2026-10-02 on the post-adjudication datasets. Arm-level haploidentical-donor percentage was available for 95% of extraction-database arms (498 of 523) and for every arm in the pooled outcome datasets (zero exclusions); missing values were never treated as zero — both analyses are complete-case. First, within-study imbalance is small: the between-arm difference in haploidentical-donor percentage has median 0 in every outcome dataset, so most of the marginal imbalance is between studies — the component absorbed by the study intercepts (and removed entirely in the fixed-intercept sensitivity above). Second, a meta-regression on the between-arm difference and a donor-matched restriction (absolute difference ≤ 15 percentage points) were fitted for each outcome. The meta-regression coefficient is near zero throughout, and the donor-matched overall-survival estimate is stronger, not weaker, than the full-set estimate (0·58 \[0·41–0·78\] versus 0·73 \[0·58–0·89\]), so the C1 survival and GVHD benefits are not driven by studies in which PTCy arms carried more haploidentical recipients. Fits and summaries are exported in `donor_confounding.csv`, a supplementary data file.

Arm-level baseline confounders vary widely in availability across the 523 extracted arms: donor-type composition 95%, conditioning intensity (MAC percentage) 89%, graft source (PBSC percentage) 85%, systemic-steroid exposure 76%, disease risk (high-risk percentage) 59%, CMV recipient serostatus 47%, donor-positive/recipient-negative serostatus 31%, and enrolment era 100% (study-level). Of these, donor type, CMV serostatus, letermovir era, and steroid exposure are addressed by dedicated analyses (this section, the CMV serostatus/letermovir section, and the exploratory M2 model); conditioning intensity, graft source, and disease risk are not adjusted for in any model, because between-study adjustment for arm-level percentages cannot remove within-study confounding and within-study imbalances were not systematically reported. This is a residual-confounding limitation of the pooled estimates.

### Randomised-trials-only analyses

The 14 randomised trials contribute to the comparisons unevenly after cohort deduplication, so these analyses use the full analytic datasets (one publication per trial cohort). The trial-only estimates previously reported here are superseded because they included cumulative-incidence-derived event counts. After those derived counts were removed from pooling (2026-10-02), trial-only analyses are **no longer estimable for any C1 outcome**: the randomised trials report Kaplan–Meier and cumulative-incidence estimates almost exclusively, and restricting to observed event counts leaves at most two trials per outcome (overall survival k = 2; acute GVHD k = 1; chronic GVHD k = 2; non-relapse mortality k = 1; CMV k = 0). The observational-only estimates below (non-trial studies only) are the post-adjudication complement and should be read alongside the explicit statement that trial evidence with observed counts is insufficient to carry the survival and GVHD conclusions independently.

| Acute GVHD II–IV | Observational only | 27 | 0·60 (0·44–0·78) |
| Chronic GVHD mod–severe | Observational only | 14 | 0·48 (0·27–0·86) |
| Non-relapse mortality | Observational only | 10 | 0·91 (0·57–1·36) |
| CMV reactivation | Observational only | 7 | 1·01 (0·64–1·64) |

### CMV serostatus and letermovir

Arm-level CMV recipient serostatus was available for only half of the CMV model arms. Letermovir status is recorded in the extraction database as confirmed use, confirmed non-use, or not reported, and the three are kept distinct throughout: of the 44 C1 CMV model arms, 28 are **confirmed non-use** and 16 are not reported; no model arm has recorded letermovir use. (Database-wide, recorded use exists — 37 arms with universal or selective use — but none of those arms contribute to the C1 CMV model.) An enrolment-era proxy (post-2018 versus earlier or era-spanning) is available for all arms and is preferable to publication year, which lags adoption. Adjusting for the era proxy leaves the CMV estimate unchanged (1·20 \[0·86–1·67\], k = 21; era coefficient −0·79 \[−1·74–0·15\] on the log-OR scale), as does adjustment for the between-arm difference in recipient seropositivity on the subset with serostatus data (1·16 \[0·64–1·97\], k = 10; coefficient 0·05 \[−0·04–0·14\] per percentage point). A meta-regression on directly reported use is not identifiable: every arm with a reported status is a confirmed non-user, so there is no exposure variation to adjust for (13 studies, 26 arms). Reconciling this with the publication-2020-onward sensitivity cohort (17 publications, 34 arms): enrolment in that cohort spans 2000–2024, largely before or across the letermovir era, and no arm has recorded use (16 confirmed non-use, 18 not reported). The larger CMV estimate in recent publications therefore cannot be attributed to — or claimed to persist despite — letermovir adoption; it is a publication-year association, not evidence about letermovir. The sensitivity subsets themselves are labelled by publication year accordingly (models and fits refitted 2026-10-02 on the post-adjudication dataset: publication-2020-onward k = 16, 1·43 \[0·97–2·06\]; haploidentical-dominant k = 12, 1·34 \[0·89–1·96\]). Fits and summaries are exported in `cmv_letermovir.csv` and `cmv_sensitivity_subsets_adj.csv`, supplementary data files.

### Comparator backbone and PTCy+ATG arms

C1 comparators mix CNI+MTX, CNI+MMF and CNI+MTX+MMF backbones. Subgroup estimates suggest the overall-survival benefit may be concentrated against CNI+MTX comparators (0·56 \[0·34–0·84\], k = 12), with no benefit against CNI+MMF (1·10 \[0·45–3·01\], k = 5) and an intermediate estimate against CNI+MTX+MMF (0·85 \[0·57–1·26\], k = 11); the acute GVHD reduction is consistent against CNI+MTX and CNI+MMF (0·53 \[0·36–0·75\] and 0·51 \[0·12–2·22\]) but attenuated against the combined backbone (0·85 \[0·45–1·57\]). However, a formal backbone × PTCy interaction model does not resolve these differences: for overall survival the ratio of odds ratios is 1·82 \[0·76–4·53\] (CNI+MMF versus CNI+MTX) and 1·46 \[0·87–2·54\] (CNI+MTX+MMF versus CNI+MTX); for acute GVHD, 1·08 \[0·48–2·46\] and 1·58 \[0·76–3·29\]; and for CMV, 0·77 \[0·28–2·52\] and 0·70 \[0·38–1·51\]. Backbone differences in the PTCy effect are therefore compatible with, but not demonstrated by, the data, and the fact that one subgroup interval excludes 1 while another does not is not itself evidence of a differential effect. Comparator mix may nonetheless contribute to the pooled C1 estimates. Arms receiving PTCy together with ATG are classified as PTCy arms in all three comparisons (54 arms database-wide; 27 C1-eligible, 8 C2-eligible, 17 C3-eligible); three C2 studies include such arms, and excluding them leaves the C2 estimates essentially unchanged (table). Fits and summaries are exported in `comparator_backbone.csv`, a supplementary data file.

### CMV outcome definitions

The reported CMV outcome is any reactivation, which rises under modern surveillance regardless of prophylaxis, whereas clinically significant CMV infection (csCMV) is the outcome letermovir-type prophylaxis is expected to change. A paired-arm csCMV dataset was built from the extraction database (8 studies, day +100 preferred, counts back-calculated from percentages where necessary, following the main pipeline's conventions). The csCMV estimate (0·94 \[0·49–1·71\]) is compatible with anything from a halving to a 71% increase in odds; with eight small, self-selected studies it is **uncertain**, and should not be read as evidence that the elevation seen for any reactivation (1·20 \[0·87–1·65\]) is absent for clinically significant infection. The two definitions answer different clinical questions and are reported separately rather than pooled. Fits and summaries are exported in `cmv_definitions.csv`, a supplementary data file.

| Clinically significant CMV infection (csCMV) |   8 | 0·94 (0·49–1·71) |
| Any CMV reactivation (reported M1)           |  22 | 1·22 (0·90–1·65) |

: CMV estimates by outcome definition, C1.

### BK virus outcome scope

The BK virus outcome in this review is **BK virus–associated haemorrhagic cystitis (BK-HC)** only. Viruria and viraemia were not extracted as outcomes, so no BK replication measures contribute to any synthesis; where a study reported both replication and cystitis, only the cystitis endpoint was taken. The label "BK virus reactivation" used for brevity in tables and figures should be read accordingly. Because BK-HC requires clinical disease (haematuria with compatible symptoms, with BK attribution per each study's criteria), it is downstream of viral replication and its incidence depends on local monitoring and diagnostic practice; definitions across the pooled studies are clinical (Bedi or ECIL grading) rather than laboratory-standardised. This scope limitation should be borne in mind when comparing the pooled BK effect with studies of BK viruria or viraemia.

### Indirect comparison of the C1 and C2 pooled effects

The depletion-depth interpretation in the main text contrasts the C1 and C2 pooled estimates. A formal indirect comparison — the posterior of the ratio of the two pooled odds ratios — is reported below. The two study sets are disjoint except for one three-arm study (Haebe 2023, study 167), whose shared contribution makes the test mildly conservative. The comparisons enrol different populations (predominantly haploidentical in C1, matched-donor in C2), so the contrast is confounded by population as well as comparator.

| Outcome | C1 OR (95% CrI) | C2 OR (95% CrI) | Ratio (95% CrI) | P(C1 \> C2) |
|:---|:---|:---|:---|---:|
| CMV reactivation | 1·22 (0·90–1·65) | 0·86 (0·50–1·42) | 1·43 (0·80–2·63) | 0·89 |
| BK virus reactivation | 2·39 (1·48–3·66) | 2·49 (1·09–6·03) | 0·95 (0·36–2·44) | 0·46 |

: Posterior indirect contrast of the pooled PTCy effects between comparisons. P(C1 \> C2) is the posterior probability that the C1 pooled effect exceeds the C2 pooled effect.

The CMV contrast is not resolved: the depletion-depth hierarchy is compatible with the data but not demonstrated by it. The BK contrast is compatible with no difference between comparators, consistent with a comparator-invariant — cyclophosphamide-specific — elevation.

### Formal comparator-class meta-regression (CMV)

As a formal test of the C1–C2 CMV difference, the C1 and C2 CMV datasets were pooled (k = 33) and refitted with a comparator-class main effect and a PTCy-by-comparator-class interaction added to the M1 specification. The interaction estimates the difference in the PTCy effect between comparator classes directly: a ratio of odds ratios of 0·71 (95% CrI 0·41–1·20) for C2 versus C1, with 90% posterior probability that the C1 effect is the larger. The difference is not resolved — the C2 estimate (0·86 \[0·55–1·32\]) is compatible with parity as well as with an intermediate position — so the depletion-depth ordering CNI-based \< PTCy \< ATG remains a hypothesis compatible with the data rather than a demonstrated hierarchy. The populations also differ (predominantly haploidentical in C1, matched-donor in C2), so comparator and population effects cannot be separated. Results are exported in `cmv_comparator_class.csv`, a supplementary data file.

## S10. Publication bias

Funnel-plot asymmetry was assessed on the post-adjudication datasets (2026-10-02; Egger's regression, Peters' sample-size test, Begg's rank test, and Duval–Tweedie trim-and-fill; full results in `pub_bias_results.csv`, supplementary data file). C1 overall survival showed asymmetry by Egger (p = 0·025) but not by the sample-size-based Peters test (p = 0·13) or Begg (p = 0·075); trim-and-fill imputed six studies, shifting the frequentist estimate from 0·75 to 0·86 \[0·70–1·07\]. C1 acute GVHD showed asymmetry across tests (Egger p = 0·023; Begg p = 0·018; Peters p = 0·072), with trim-and-fill shifting the estimate from 0·61 to 0·83 \[0·61–1·13\]. No other outcome showed significant asymmetry (all p \> 0·07). These null results should not be interpreted as evidence that bias is absent: with k = 6–13 studies the funnel-based tests have low power, and the corresponding RoBMA inclusion Bayes factors below 1 indicate at most weak evidence against publication bias for those outcomes.

Robust Bayesian model-averaging (RoBMA v4.0.0; ensemble of selection-function, PET, and PEESE publication-bias models) was fitted to every outcome with k ≥ 6 on the cohort-deduplicated datasets. Model-averaged estimates and inclusion Bayes factors for the presence of an effect (BF~eff~) and of publication bias (BF~bias~) are shown below. All ensembles converged (R̂ ≤ 1·01; ESS \> 1000).

: RoBMA model-averaged estimates, refitted 2026-10-02 on the post-adjudication datasets (cumulative-incidence- and Kaplan–Meier-derived event counts excluded; `scripts/refit-robma-adjudicated.R`). BF~eff~ and BF~bias~ are inclusion Bayes factors for the presence of an effect and of publication bias, respectively; values \> 3 are conventionally taken as moderate, \> 10 as strong evidence. Bloodstream infection is not shown: following the change of the primary BSI analysis to the culture-confirmed day-100 subset (k = 4; S9), a model-averaged publication-bias assessment is not interpretable at k = 4. The funnel-plot tests above were computed on the pre-adjudication Set B datasets and are retained for reference.

Three findings stand out. First, publication bias is supported only for the two headline C1 benefit outcomes — overall survival (BF~bias~ 10·4) and acute GVHD (BF~bias~ 10·9) — and for both, the bias-adjusted model-averaged estimate is essentially null (OS 0·97 \[0·71–1·16\]; aGVHD 0·96 \[0·57–1·38\]), consistent with the trim-and-fill results above. Second, BK virus reactivation is the only outcome with strong evidence of a non-null effect after model-averaging (BF~eff~ 9·5; adjusted estimate 1·97 \[1·00–3·13\]), with no evidence of bias; moderate effect evidence supports chronic GVHD (BF~eff~ 5·4 moderate–severe, 4·5 any), with weak-to-moderate bias evidence for the any-definition subset (BF~bias~ 5·3). Third, no other outcome yielded more than weak evidence for either an effect or publication bias. The RoBMA results should temper confidence in the unadjusted C1 survival and acute GVHD estimates reported in table 2.

## S11. GRADE certainty-of-evidence profiles

Certainty was assessed per the GRADE Handbook, adapted for observational evidence (starting certainty LOW). The profiles below were reassessed (2026-10-02) against the post-adjudication, random-slope estimates of table 2 and the refitted publication-bias analyses of S10, and supersede all earlier profiles. **Risk of bias.** Two-thirds (68%) of contributing observational studies are at serious risk of bias by ROBINS-I (S5); the evidence therefore starts at LOW for observational designs, and no further risk-of-bias downgrade is applied beyond the starting level except for C1 NRM (steroid-mediation confounding). The randomised trials are too few to shift any pooled estimate materially (S9), so their generally lower risk of bias does not raise the rating for any outcome. **Indirectness.** No outcome is downgraded for indirectness; qualifications are noted per row (any-CMV-reactivation as a surrogate for clinically significant infection; BK measured as haemorrhagic cystitis rather than viral replication; predominantly haploidentical C1 versus matched-donor C2 populations). **Imprecision** is assessed against pre-specified clinically meaningful thresholds (odds ratio 0·80 for benefit, 1·25 for harm): a downgrade is applied when the 95% credible interval spans the relevant threshold or the null.

Starting certainty LOW (observational evidence; 68% of contributing studies at serious ROBINS-I risk). Imprecision is assessed against clinically meaningful thresholds (OR 0·80 benefit, 1·25 harm). On this reassessment C1 relapse-related mortality moves from LOW to VERY LOW (its interval spans the 0·80 threshold); C1 BK virus remains LOW (interval entirely above 1·25). C2 BSI and C2 IFI were not modelled (insufficient studies) and are not rated. The final six rows cover the secondary outcomes added by protocol amendment (BK virus reactivation, infection-related mortality, relapse-related mortality; S13), rated under the same framework; C3 outcomes were not rated.

### Summary-of-findings absolute effects

Odds ratios are not relative risks, and relative measures alone can mislead at the event rates seen here. The table below translates each pooled odds ratio into an absolute difference per 1000 patients at the stated baseline risk (the median comparator-arm event proportion across included studies). These are illustrative translations of the odds ratios, not model-based risk estimates, and inherit the very low certainty of the underlying evidence.

| Outcome | Comparison | Time horizon | Assumed baseline risk | OR (95% CrI) | Absolute difference per 1000 (95% CrI) |
|:---|:---|:---|---:|:---|---:|
| Overall survival (mortality) | C1 | 1 year (2-yr/last follow-up fallbacks) | 35% | 0·73 (0·58–0·89) | −68 (−111 to −26) |
| Overall survival (mortality) | C2 | 1 year (2-yr fallback) | 52% | 0·75 (0·43–1·28) | −71 (−204 to +61) |
| Non-relapse mortality | C1 | 1 year (day +100/last follow-up fallbacks) | 16% | 0·84 (0·48–1·28) | −22 (−77 to +37) |
| Acute GVHD II–IV | C1 | day +100 (day +180 fallback) | 33% | 0·58 (0·44–0·76) | −108 (−155 to −58) |
| Acute GVHD II–IV | C2 | day +100 (day +180 fallback) | 40% | 0·53 (0·23–1·17) | −138 (−266 to +38) |
| CMV reactivation | C1 | day +100 (day +180/last follow-up fallbacks) | 48% | 1·20 (0·87–1·65) | +46 (−35 to +123) |
| CMV reactivation | C2 | day +100 (day +180 fallback) | 47% | 0·86 (0·51–1·42) | −38 (−160 to +88) |
| Bloodstream infection | C1 | day +100 (culture-confirmed primary) | 21% | 2·17 (0·86–4·39) | +154 (−24 to +326) |
| Invasive fungal infection | C1 | end of follow-up | 14% | 0·63 (0·19–2·44) | −48 (−111 to +146) |

: Summary-of-findings absolute effects with uncertainty intervals and explicit time horizons (the preferred timepoint of each outcome's analysis, with fallback timepoints in parentheses). Baseline risk is the median comparator-arm event proportion at that horizon; the intervention risk is derived from the pooled odds ratio as OR·p₀/(1−p₀+OR·p₀). Negative values are fewer events with PTCy. Source data: `absolute_effects.csv`, a supplementary data file.

## S12. Cohort overlap

![Cohort overlap map. Studies sharing patient cohorts were flagged and the most comprehensive publication designated as primary for each cohort–outcome combination (Set B, the adopted analysis).](figures/FigureS12_cohort_overlap_map){#fig-s12}

During revision, one publication (Wu 2025, *British Journal of Haematology*; doi 10.1111/bjh.70133) was found to have been entered twice in the extraction database (study identifiers 395 and 401, assigned separate cohort identifiers 1154 and 1158). The duplicate entry was removed. All counts, analyses, tables, and figures in this revision use the corrected database (250 studies, 523 arms; C1 overall survival k = 34).

### Per-outcome attrition from extraction to pooling

The pooled study count is smaller than the comparison size for every outcome because the models require a harmonised timepoint with actual event counts per arm, and because cohort deduplication (Set B) retains one publication per cohort. The table below gives, for each outcome, the number of studies with paired-arm outcome records in the extraction database and the number pooled in the reported model.

| Comparison | Outcome | Studies with paired-arm records | Studies pooled |
|:---|:---|---:|---:|
| C1 | Overall survival | 116 | 34 |
| C1 | Non-relapse mortality | 109 | 12 |
| C1 | Relapse-related mortality | 41 | 34 |
| C1 | Acute GVHD II–IV | 104 | 28 |
| C1 | Chronic GVHD mod–severe | 61 | 19 |
| C1 | Chronic GVHD any | 28 | 8 |
| C1 | CMV reactivation | 46 | 22 |
| C1 | Bloodstream infection | 13 | 4 |
| C1 | Invasive fungal infection | 7 | 6 |
| C1 | BK virus | 27 | 11 |
| C1 | Infection-related mortality | 18 | 13 |
| C2 | Overall survival | 47 | 9 |
| C2 | Non-relapse mortality | 43 | 3 |
| C2 | Relapse-related mortality | 12 | 10 |
| C2 | Acute GVHD II–IV | 43 | 8 |
| C2 | Chronic GVHD mod–severe | 26 | 6 |
| C2 | CMV reactivation | 18 | 12 |
| C2 | BK virus | 10 | 3 |
| C2 | Infection-related mortality | 9 | 7 |
| C3 | Overall survival | 18 | 6 |
| C3 | Non-relapse mortality | 18 | 5 |
| C3 | Relapse-related mortality | 6 | 6 |
| C3 | Acute GVHD II–IV | 18 | 7 |
| C3 | Chronic GVHD mod–severe | 14 | 4 |

: Per-outcome attrition. "Studies with paired-arm records" counts studies with extractable event data (counts or percentages) for both a PTCy and an eligible comparator arm in `outcomes.csv`; "studies pooled" is the model-input k from table 2. The difference reflects outcome-specific eligibility (harmonised timepoint, actual event counts rather than derived estimates), complete-case rules, and — for the seven deduplication-affected outcomes below — removal of duplicate cohort publications. A small number of pooled studies enter via rebuilt estimates (for example from reported hazard ratios) and so do not appear in the extracted-count column. Source data: `outcome_flow.csv`, a supplementary data file.

### Estimates before and after cohort deduplication

Cohort deduplication (Set B) changed seven outcomes; all other outcomes were unaffected. Set A values are the pre-deduplication estimates under the originally submitted common-effect model; Set B values are the reported estimates under the random-slope model (the specification change is documented in S6 and S9). Note that the Set A C1 overall-survival M2 result (0·86 \[0·77–0·96\]) was originally read as a residual direct survival benefit; under Set B the steroid-adjusted estimate is 0·96 \[0·72–1·28\], and M2 is now reported as an appendix-only exploratory analysis (S9).

| Outcome | k, Set A | OR, Set A (common-effect) | k, Set B | OR, Set B (reported) |

| C1 Overall survival (M2, appendix-only) | 40 | 0·86 (0·77–0·96) | 27 | 0·95 (0·70–1·27) |
| C1 Relapse-related mortality | 38 | 0·84 (0·76–0·93) | 34 | 0·87 (0·76–0·99) |
| C1 Chronic GVHD mod–severe | 21 | 0·33 (0·29–0·36) | 19 | 0·40 (0·22–0·68) |
| C1 Infection-related mortality | 16 | 1·35 (1·16–1·57) | 13 | 1·03 (0·68–1·49) |
| C2 Overall survival | 10 | 0·81 (0·74–0·90) | 9 | 0·75 (0·42–1·31) |
| C2 Acute GVHD II–IV | 9 | 0·58 (0·44–0·77) | 8 | 0·51 (0·24–1·02) |
| C2 CMV reactivation | 13 | 0·92 (0·73–1·15) | 12 | 0·86 (0·50–1·42) |

## S13. PROSPERO registration

The study protocol was registered with PROSPERO (CRD420261372156) before data extraction. Protocol amendments were: (1) a Bayesian rather than frequentist primary analysis framework; (2) addition of BK virus reactivation, infection-related mortality, and relapse-related mortality as secondary outcomes; and (3) addition of the steroid-adjustment (M2) model as an exploratory analysis.

## S15. Software and statistical packages used

All analyses were performed in R (versions 4·6·0 and 4·6·1; R: A Language and Environment for Statistical Computing, R Foundation for Statistical Computing, Vienna, Austria) [@rcoreteam2026]. Bayesian models were fitted with Stan via `brms` [@burkner2017; @burkner2018; @carpenter2017]; frequentist concordance models used `metafor` [@viechtbauer2010]; publication-bias assessment used `RoBMA` [@bartos2020]; data manipulation used the `tidyverse` packages [@wickham2019]. Documents were rendered with Quarto (version 1.10.18).

| Package | Version | Role |
|:---|:---|:---|
| brms | 2.23.0 | Bayesian binomial-logistic meta-analysis models (M1, M2, and all sensitivity models) |
| rstan | 2.32.7 | MCMC sampling backend; convergence diagnostics (R̂, effective sample sizes, divergences) |
| StanHeaders | 2.39.1 | Stan model compilation |
| posterior | 1.7.0 | Posterior draw handling and summaries |
| metafor | 5.2.1 | Frequentist REML concordance models, leave-one-out analysis, log-odds-ratio calculations |
| RoBMA | 4.0.0 | Robust Bayesian model-averaging assessment of publication bias |
| bayesplot | 1.16.0 | MCMC diagnostic figures (trace plots, posterior densities) |
| ggplot2 | 4.0.3 | All figures |
| ggridges | 0.5.7 | τ posterior density figure |
| patchwork | 1.3.2 | Multi-panel figure composition and forest-plot side tables |
| scales | 1.4.0 | Axis and percentage formatting |
| PRISMA2020 | 1.1.5 | PRISMA 2020 flow diagram (figure 1) |
| knitr | 1.52 | Tables in source notebooks |
| dplyr | 1.2.1 | Data manipulation |
| tidyr | 1.3.2 | Data reshaping |
| readr | 2.2.0 | Data import |
| purrr | 1.2.2 | Iteration |
| stringr | 1.6.0 | String formatting |
| tibble | 3.3.1 | Data frames |
| forcats | 1.0.1 | Factor handling |
